Photograph: J Scott Applewhite/AP Ilhan Omar Ilhan Omar’s attorneys say federal search of her home was ‘neither justified nor lawful’ Minnesota lawmaker’s attorneys asked for return of seized items and the preservation of any recordings of search Eric Berger and agencies Sat 17 Oct 2026 10.21 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Ilhan Omar ’s attorneys have asked the US Department of Justice to return property that federal agents removed days earlier from her home during a search. The lawyers for the Minnesota Democrat contended that the seizure as “neither justified nor lawful”, according to a letter that the Associated Press reported on Friday. The federal investigation into Omar was launched just weeks ahead of the 3 November midterms, in which Omar is on the ballot. Democrats accused Donald Trump, a Republican, of abusing his power as president to target a political opponent. Ilhan Omar’s phone seized and relatives subpoenaed in criminal inquiry, source says Read more Omar’s attorneys wrote that there is “no legitimate basis for any suggestion that she has violated any law concerning her citizenship status”, according to the Wall Street Journal , which first reported on the lawyers’ letter. “This vindictive, retributive, and politically motivated criminal investigation into one of the president’s chief congressional critics violates Representative Omar’s constitutional rights and threatens the separation of powers,” the congresswoman’s attorneys wrote. The federal government has issued more than a dozen grand jury subpoenas, including of Omar’s relatives, and seized her phone in its investigation of the congresswoman. A justice department spokesperson said the letter from Omar’s defense team was “riddled with false allegations and inaccuracies”, according to the AP. “Our attorneys and law enforcement partners complied with all court orders and legal obligations, as they always do,” the spokesperson, Emily Covington, wrote in a text message on Friday evening. The letter from Omar’s lawyers also accused the justice department of violating the agency’s longstanding policy aimed at avoiding potentially influencing an election. And they raised concerns about whether the investigators followed instructions from the magistrate judge who approved the search. The attorneys demanded in the letter that the justice department preserve any audio and video taken during the search on Monday. The justice department launched the investigation after years of Trump and conservative media figures promoting unsubstantiated rumors that Omar’s ex-husband is actually her brother – and that she married him so that he could obtain immigration status. Omar, the most prominent Somali American in the US, has denied that allegation. Citing sources “close to the investigation”, Fox News reported that the search on Monday was related to a criminal fraud investigation concerning Omar’s immigration paperwork. Omar’s father filled out that paperwork when she was a child. “I’m ok,” Omar posted on X after the raid. “Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement.” Omar also said the search was “just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation”. The president has consistently launched racist attacks against Omar and other Somali Americans in Minnesota . In December, he described them as “garbage” who “come from hell, and they complain, and do nothing but bitch”. He said Omar “should be thrown the hell out of our country”. After Monday’s search, Trump denied being involved in the investigation. “I’ve always found her to be totally crooked, personally, but that has nothing to do with me,” Trump said. https://hvg.hu/vilag/20261114_orosz-ukra.text: Az oroszok nem sokkal az őket ért csapások után ukrán városokat vettek célba. Súlyos csapást mértek az ukránok egy orosz olajlétesítményre, valamint egy katonai repülőtérre. A Szamara megyében található, Szamara elnevezésű lineáris termelési és diszpécserállomás fontos csomópontja az orosz olajszállítási rendszernek. Itt keverik össze az elsősorban Tatárföldről és Nyugat-Szibériából kapott nyersolajat, hogy előállítsák az Urals nevű exportolajat. A beszámoló szerint a támadás következtében több olajtároló tartály is felgyulladt. Az ukránok emellett egy Lipeck közelében található katonai repülőteret is támadtak. Itt egy hangár, egy repülőgép-üzemanyagtartály, valamint a légiirányító központ eltalálásáról számoltak be. Az MTI beszámolója szerint szombat délelőtt az oroszok ukrán polgári infrastrukturális épületet támadtak Zaporizzsja városában. A katasztrófavédelem szerint 22-en sebesültek meg a várost ért orosz támadásokban, köztük egy hat hónapos csecsemő, egy kétéves kislány és egy 12 éves fiú. Szombaton emellett Pavlohrad városát is orosz csapás érte, itt egy ember meghalt, tízen pedig megsebesültek. 5 071 632 000 forint, 2 658 350 euró, 1 257 100 dollár.

https://www.politico.eu/article/commissi.text: LUXEMBOURG — The European Commission was accused Wednesday of withholding internal messages that explain why it dropped a contentious patent proposal, amid claims of pressure from U.S. Vice President JD Vance. At a court hearing in Luxembourg, judges were told that German center-left MEP Tiemo Wölken asked the Commission for internal notes on why the proposal was abruptly killed in early 2025. He was told there was only one relevant internal document: minutes of a private meeting between heads of cabinet, which the Commission refused to hand over. Wölken’s lawyers said the absence of information was hard to believe given how contentious the proposal had become. Advertisement Advertisement It was “unbelievable” that there were “zero emails on this highly-politicized, economically-relevant procedure,” Carsten Zatschler, Wölken’s lawyer, said at the EU's General Court. “All of this apparently happened without any form of electronic communication,” Zatschler said. “That’s quite simply not credible.” In February 2025, the Commission announced it was withdrawing plans for a standard essential patents (SEPs) regulation on the licensing of patents, saying there was no “clear signal of support” from co-legislators. Negotiations between the European Parliament and EU countries were ongoing at the time. The proposal was officially killed in July that year. The proposal had triggered a fierce lobbying battle between patent holders — including Nokia, Ericsson, Qualcomm and Huawei — and companies that license their technology, from phone makers to carmakers. The withdrawal was announced on the same day that Vance met with Commission President Ursula von der Leyen at an AI summit in Paris, where they discussed AI, Ukraine and transatlantic ties. The timing prompted questions in the European Parliament about whether their conversation played a role in quashing the proposal. Zatschler asked: “Why was it surprisingly withdrawn? Whether a meeting between Ursula von der Leyen and U.S. Vice President JD Vance played a role, that's obviously not something we need to discuss here.” Advertisement Advertisement “But whether it can be clarified should not be dependent on whether the European Commission categorized emails as important or not, because otherwise we would be putting the fox in charge of the hen house,” he said. Wölken was part of the negotiating team blindsided by the decision. “My team had met the Polish presidency [of the Council of the EU] just days before, and they were gearing up to finalize the Council position,” the lawmaker told POLITICO. “No one was informed.” “That alone raises questions about the withdrawal, which for me turned into a real concern after hearing rumors about the meeting between Ursula von der Leyen and JD Vance,” he said. The Commission did hand over 14 documents to the German MEP, most of which were emails and position papers from outside stakeholders sent to the Commission after the decision to kill the proposal was announced. Lawyers for the Commission told judges that Wölken's request didn’t specify that he was seekend internal emails predating the decision. Advertisement Advertisement “These are professional lawyers,” said Tim Maxian Rusche, representing the Commission (Wölken is also a lawyer). “They work directly in Brussels. If they want internal correspondence, they’re going to have to specify that.” He added that the Commission is “being exposed to more and more fishing expeditions” where it is asked “very general” questions in access to document requests. “They need to make [requests] clear, because otherwise we can’t do our work,” he continued. The Commission is also facing a lawsuit from the European Parliament over the decision to kill the proposal. Last year, lawmakers voted to sue the Commission over the decision, arguing that it had overstepped its competence. “The Commission’s right to withdraw a proposal ... cannot be used as a political instrument to short-circuit Parliament’s work or to enforce a deregulation agenda from above,” German Social Democrat René Repasi said. “This is not in line with how the democratic processes in the European Union are meant to function.” The judges did not confirm when a decision would be made in the case.
